description: Ecliptic Nomads: turning NASA open data into tools for the next frontier.
summary: After the magnitude 7.7 earthquake in Panama on 9 October 2026, clouds and thick forest hid landslides from normal satellites, so it was hard to know which roads were blocked and which communities were cut off. Cut Off uses NISAR L-band radar, which can collect images through cloud and at night, to find leads. We compared NISAR images from before and after the quake and looked for forested slopes where the radar signal dropped more than the ground around it. We then joined these candidate landslides to the OpenStreetMap road network. The website shows roads that are likely blocked and communities that are possibly cut off on a map with a before/after swipe of radar and optical images. This helps first responders and planners decide where to look first. We also tested the method on hand-marked points and a pre-event baseline, and we show the results next to the numbers, including the weak spots. It found 33% of held-out landslide points. Candidates are leads, not confirmed landslides, and this is a research demo, not an official warning.
details:
What it does

After the magnitude 7.7 earthquake in Panama on 9 October 2026, the first question for responders is which roads are blocked and which villages can’t be reached. Landslides are a big part of the answer, but clouds and thick forest hide them from normal satellites. Cut Off uses NISAR L-band radar to look for leads. Radar can collect images through cloud and at night.

We compared NISAR images from before and after the quake, on four before/after pairs from different passes and a pre-event baseline. We looked for forested slopes where the radar signal dropped more than the ground around it. We then joined those candidate landslides to the OpenStreetMap road network. A road is “likely blocked” if a candidate touches it. A community is “possibly cut off” if every mapped road from it to a nearby town crosses a likely-blocked road. The website shows all of this on a map with a before/after swipe of radar and Sentinel-2 optical images. It also lists the communities with a reason for each status.

How it works

All processing runs offline in Python. The website and API only read the result files, so nothing heavy runs in the browser. The steps are:

  1. Compute the change in the HV radar signal on a 20 m grid.
  2. Subtract each pair’s own local average change, so region-wide effects like wetter soil are not counted as landslides.
  3. Keep pixels flagged by two passes where two passes can see them.
  4. Drop patches under 3 pixels.
  5. Mark slopes the radar can’t see (shadow and layover) as unknown rather than clear.

The result is 8,442 candidate landslides covering 19.1 km². They give 92.2 km of road likely blocked and 102 of 460 mapped places possibly cut off.

How we tested it, and what we found

We marked 183 check points on Sentinel-2 images, fresh landslide scars and untouched forest, and checked every one by eye. The radar was never used to pick them. We split them in half at random, chose the method settings on one half, and kept the other half held out. On the held-out half, the first version of our method found 12 of 57 landslide points (21%, AUC 0.55). After we revised it using only the tuning half, it found 19 of 57 (33%) and flagged 0 of 34 forest points (AUC 0.86). We score the held-out half twice and show both results on the website and in the README. We also ran the method on two passes from before the quake: it flagged 3.3% of forested slope against 4.8% after the quake, so the separation is real but modest.

We are open about what this is not. It is a random split in one study area, labelled from optical images, so it is not independent validation or field validation. Most check-point landslides are smaller than 100 m, close to the radar pixel size, so many are missed. Candidates are leads to verify, not confirmed landslides. “Likely blocked” is inferred from a landslide beside a road, and nobody saw the blockages. The NISAR data are PROVISIONAL. This is a research demo, not an official warning.

Benefits and intended impact

The aim is a fast, transparent first list of places to check in the first days after an earthquake, when clouds make optical imagery unreliable. Just as important, it shows how far the list can be trusted, so a reader can decide how to use it. The code, the result files and a read-only API are all open, and the pipeline is driven by a configuration file, so it can be rerun on other earthquakes with NISAR data.

What is creative about it

Most radar-landslide demos stop at a map. Ours puts the accuracy check next to the headline numbers: both scorings of the held-out points, a pre-event baseline, and a per-size breakdown. The local-average correction makes the before-the-quake and after-the-quake comparison fair. The weak points are on the first screen, not hidden in a footnote.

Tools

Python (NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, NetworkX, rasterio, Shapely, GeoPandas), FastAPI in a Docker container on Azure App Service, and a React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS website with MapLibre GL JS, hosted on Cloudflare. We also used GitHub Actions for tests and deployment, and Lighthouse to check performance and accessibility. The site works on a phone (checked at 390 px) and has no trackers.

What we considered

Provisional data, radar speckle, shadow and layover, the 12-day gap between passes, missing roads in OpenStreetMap, and the risk of overclaiming. That last one is why the wording is always “candidate”, “likely blocked” and “possibly cut off”. AI tools helped with code, text drafts and suggesting check points. Every check point was verified by eye and every result comes from our own processing. See the AI-use log in the repository.
